# The Linear Model

Last week ended with a trick question. You ran a t-test, you ran a correlation, and then you ran `lm()` — and the numbers came back the same. That was not a coincidence, and this week we find out why.

Here is the idea the rest of the course rests on: **almost everything we do is a line through data.** A group difference is a line. A correlation is a line. Regression is not a new topic sitting next to t-tests and correlations — it is the general machine that those tests are special cases of. Once you can read a line, you can read most of a results section.

So this week we slow down on three numbers: the **intercept** (where the line starts), the **slope** (how steeply it climbs), and the **residual** (how wrong the line is for one particular person). We'll fold in correlation and effect size along the way, because *r* and R² are just other ways of asking how much the line helps.

::: callout-note
## A note on the intercept

You are about to meet a lot of intercepts that are nonsense — the predicted number of Transformers movies for a person aged zero, the price of a LEGO set with no pieces. That is fine and expected. Part of reading a model well is knowing which of its numbers you are allowed to take seriously.
:::
